'''affectedly''' (ạ-fek′ted-li), ''adv.'' 1. In an affected or assumed manner; with affectation; hypocritically; with more show than reality: as, to walk ''affectedly; affectedly'' civil.
{{smaller block|Balzac was genuinely as well as ''affectedly'' monarchical, and he was saturated with a sense of the past.
{{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Little Tour, p. 7.}}}}
2†. With tender care; lovingly.
{{smaller block|<poem>Letters sadly penn’d in blood,
With sleided silk feat and ''affectedly''
Enswathed.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lover’s Complaint, l. 48.}}}}

'''affectedness''' (ạ-fek′ted-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being affected; affectation.

'''affecter''' (ạ-fek′tėr), ''n.'' [< ''affect''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] 1. One who affects, pretends, or assumes.—2†. One who affects or loves.
{{smaller block|<poem>Bring forth the princess dress’d in royal robes,
The true ''affecter'' of Alvero’s son.</poem>
{{right|''Lust’s Dominion'', v. 1.}}}}

Also spelled ''affector.''

'''affectibility''' (ạ-fek-ti-bil′ị-ti), ''n.'' The state of being affectible.

'''affectible''' (ạ-fek′ti-bl), ''a.'' [< ''affect''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ible.''] Capable of being affected. [Rare.]

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|affectate|98|affectuous}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''affectate†''' (a-fek′tāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''affectatus'', pp. of ''affectare'': see ''affect''<sup>1</sup>.] Affected; marked by affectation. ''Elyot'', Dict.

'''affectation''' (af-ek-tā′shọn), ''n.'' [< L. ''affectatio(n-)'', ''adfectatio(n-)'', a striving after, affectation, conceit, < ''affectare'', ''adfectare'', strive after, affect, imitate: see ''affect''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1†.''' Strenuous pursuit or desire; earnest quest; a striving in the direction (of).
{{smaller block|Pretended sedition and ''affectation'' of the crown.
{{right|''Bp. Pearson'', Expos. of Creed, p. 293.}}
The ''affectation'' of being Gay and in Fashion has very nearly eaten up our Good Sense and our Religion.
{{right|''Steele'', Spectator.}}}}
'''2.''' A striving for the appearance (of); pretense of the possession or character (of); effort for the reputation (of): as, an ''affectation'' of wit or of virtue; ''affectation'' of great wealth.
{{smaller block|His arguments are stated with the utmost ''affectation'' of precision.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Mill on Government.}}
In matters of taste the Anglo-Saxon mind seems always to have felt a painful distrust of itself, which it betrays either in an ''affectation'' of burly contempt or in a pretence of admiration equally insincere.
{{right|''Lowell'', Study Windows, p. 395.}}}}
'''3.''' A striving for effect; artificiality of manner or conduct; effort to attract notice by pretense, assumption, or any peculiarity: as, his ''affectations'' are insufferable.
{{smaller block|''Affectation'' is an awkward and forced imitation of what should be genuine and easy, wanting the beauty that accompanies what is natural.
{{right|''Locke'', Education.}}
The good sense and good taste which had weeded out ''affectation'' from moral and political treatises would, in the natural course of things, have effected a similar reform in the sonnet and the ode.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Dryden.}}}} 4'''†'''. Affection; fondness.
{{smaller block|Bonds of ''affectation'' . . . between man and wife.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Cases of Conscience, iv. 3.}}}}

'''affectationist''' (af-ek-tā′sho̤n-ist), ''n.'' [< ''affectation'' + ''-ist.''] One who indulges in affectation; one who is given to putting on airs.
{{smaller block|It is just the kind of phrase to be petted, as it is, by certain ''affectationists.'' {{right|''F. Hall'', Mod. Eng., p. 94.}}}}

'''affected<sup>1</sup>''' (a̤-fek′ted), ''p. a.'' [< ''affect''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1'''†. Beloved: as, “his ''affected'' Hercules,” ''Chapman'', Iliad, viii. 318.—'''2.''' Having an affection, disposition, or inclination of any kind; inclined or disposed: as, well ''affected'' to government or toward a project.
{{smaller block|Made their minds evil ''affected'' against the brethren.
{{right|Acts xiv. 2.}}
How he doth stand ''affected'' to our purpose.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iii. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' Assumed artificially; not natural: as, ''affected'' airs.
{{smaller block|Of all his epistles, the least ''affected'' are those addressed to the dead or the unborn. {{right|''Macaulay'', Petrarch.}}}}
'''4.''' Given to affectation; assuming or pretending to possess characteristics which are not natural or real: as, an ''affected'' lady.
{{smaller block|Olivia was often ''affected'', from too great a desire to please. {{right|''Goldsmith'', Vicar, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|='''Syn.''' '''3.''' Artificial, feigned, insincere.—'''4.''' Pretentious, self-conscious.}}

'''affected<sup>2</sup>''' (a̤-fek′ted), ''p. a.'' [< ''affect''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>; partly merged in ''affected''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Acted upon; influenced; particularly, influenced injuriously; impaired; attacked, as by climate or disease.—'''2.''' In ''alg.'', same as ''adfected.''—'''3.''' In the ''Rom. Cath. Ch.'', said of a benefice the collation of which is reserved to persons possessed of certain qualifications; specifically, when the pope, by some disposition of the benefice, prevents the regular collation and tacitly signifies his intention of himself providing for the benefice when it shall become vacant.

'''affectedly''' (ạ-fek′ted-li), ''adv.'' 1. In an affected or assumed manner; with affectation; hypocritically; with more show than reality: as, to walk ''affectedly; affectedly'' civil.
{{smaller block|Balzac was genuinely as well as ''affectedly'' monarchical, and he was saturated with a sense of the past.
{{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Little Tour, p. 7.}}}}
2†. With tender care; lovingly.
{{smaller block|<poem>Letters sadly penn’d in blood,
With sleided silk feat and ''affectedly''
Enswathed.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lover’s Complaint, l. 48.}}}}

'''affectedness''' (ạ-fek′ted-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being affected; affectation.

'''affecter''' (ạ-fek′tėr), ''n.'' [< ''affect''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] 1. One who affects, pretends, or assumes.—2†. One who affects or loves.
{{smaller block|<poem>Bring forth the princess dress’d in royal robes,
The true ''affecter'' of Alvero’s son.</poem>
{{right|''Lust’s Dominion'', v. 1.}}}}

Also spelled ''affector.''

'''affectibility''' (ạ-fek-ti-bil′ị-ti), ''n.'' The state of being affectible.

'''affectible''' (ạ-fek′ti-bl), ''a.'' [< ''affect''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ible.''] Capable of being affected. [Rare.]

'''affecting'''<sup>1</sup>† (a̤-fek′ting), ''p. a.'' [Ppr. of ''affect''<sup>1</sup>.] 1. Loving; affectionate.—2. Using affectation; affected.
{{smaller block|I never heard such a drawling-''affecting'' rogue.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., ii. 1.}}}}

'''affecting'''<sup>2</sup> (a̤-fek′ting), ''p. a.'' [Ppr. of ''affect''<sup>2</sup>.] Having power to excite or move the feelings; tending to move the affections; pathetic: as, an ''affecting'' spectacle; an ''affecting'' speech.
{{smaller block|I suppose you are surprised that I am not more sorrowful at parting with so many near relations; to be sure 'tis very ''affecting''. {{right|''Sheridan'', School for Scandal, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller|= '''Syn.''' Moving, touching, impressive, stirring.}}

'''affectingly''' (a̤-fek′ting-li), ''adv.'' In an affecting manner; in a manner to excite emotion.

'''affection''' (a̤-fek′sho̤n), ''n.'' [< ME. ''affectiun'', ''affection'', < OF. ''affection'', < L. ''affectio(n-)'', a state of mind or feeling, especially a favorable state, love, affection, < ''afficere'', ''adficere'', act upon, influence: see ''affect''<sup>2</sup>. ''Affection'' is formally a deriv. of ''affect''<sup>2</sup>, but in usage it rests also in part on ''affect''<sup>1</sup>.] 1. The state of having one’s feelings affected; bent or disposition of mind; phase of mental disposition; feeling.
{{smaller block|Beware chiefly of two ''affections'', fear and love.
{{right|''Latimer'', 2d Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1550.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Affection'' is applicable to an unpleasant as well as a pleasant state of the mind when impressed by any object or quality. {{right|''Cogan'', On the Passions, i. § 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Specifically—(''a'') A general name for that class of feelings which bear an immediate relation of attraction or hostility toward other persons, and even toward things, as love, esteem, gratitude, hatred, jealousy, etc. This use of the term is most frequent in ethical discussions, as in the common distinction between ''benevolent'' and ''malevolent'' affections.}}

{{smaller block|The ''affections'' and the reason are both undoubtedly necessary factors in morality, but the initiation is not in the reason, but in the ''affections''.
{{right|''Fowler'', Shaftesbury and Hutcheson, p. 217.}}}}
{{smaller block|The hues of sunset make life great; so the ''affections'' make some little web of cottage and fireside populous, important, and filling the main space in our history.
{{right|''Emerson'', Success.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Desire; inclination; appetite; propensity, good or evil: as, virtuous or vile ''affections''. Rom. i. 26; Gal. v. 24. (''c''†) One of the passions or violent emotions.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Most wretched man,
That to ''affections'' does the bridle lend.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. iv. 34.}}}}

2. A settled good will, love, or zealous attachment: as, the ''affection'' of a parent for his child: generally followed by ''for'', sometimes by ''to'' or ''toward'', before the object.
{{smaller block|''Affection'' turn’d to hatred threatens mischief.
{{right|''Ford'', Lady’s Trial, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|[Essex] desired to inspire, not gratitude, but ''affection''.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Lord Bacon.}}}}
{{smaller block|I think no modern writer has inspired his readers with such ''affection to'' his own personality.
{{right|''Emerson'', Sir W. Scott.}}}}

3†. Natural instinct or impulse; sympathy.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Affection'',
Master of passion, sways it to the mood
Of what it likes, or loathes. ''Shak.'', M. of V., iv. 1.</poem>}}

4†. Prejudice; bias.
{{smaller block|"Well," he says, “a woman may not reign in England.” “Better in England than anywhere, as it shall well appear to him that without ''affection'' will consider the kind of regiment.” ''Bp. Aylmer'', Harborough for Faithful Subjects.}}

5. A modification; the effect or result of action upon a thing; especially, in ''psychol.'', a passive modification of consciousness. {{smaller block|All ''affections'' of consciousness we term sensations.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Social Statics, p. 91.}}}}
6. In ''metaph.'' (translation of Gr. πάθος, suffering), one of those qualities of bodies by which they directly affect the senses: often improperly extended to other properties of bodies.
{{smaller block|I distinguish extension and figure by the title of the mathematical ''affections'' of matter. {{right|''D. Stewart.''}}}}
{{smaller block|The so-called forces of nature have been well and truly spoken of as the moods or ''affections'' of matter.
{{right|''W. L. Carpenter'', Energy in Nature, p. 1.}}}}
7. A disease, or the condition of being diseased; a morbid or abnormal state of body or mind: as, a gouty ''affection''; hysteric ''affection''.
{{smaller block|<poem>And, truly, waking dreams were, more or less,
An old and strange ''affection'' of the house.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', The Princess, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|I have been thinking . . . of the singular ''affection'' to which you are subject.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Mortal Antipathy, xxi.}}}}
8. In ''painting'', a lively representation of passion. ''Wotton.'' [Rare.]—9†. Affectation.
{{smaller block|Pleasant without scurrility, witty without ''affection''.
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|=Syn. 2. ''Attachment, Fondness'', etc. (see ''love''), tenderness, partiality, bias. See ''passion''.}}

'''affection''' (a-fek′shon), ''v. t.'' [= F. ''affectionner''; from the noun.] To love; have an affection for. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|But can you ''affection'' the 'oman?
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., i. 1.}}}}

'''affectional''' (a̤-fek′shọn-al), ''a.'' Relating to or implying affection; relating to the affections.
{{smaller block|God has made women, as men, compound creatures, with a fivefold nature; and it cannot be that either side, physical, mental, moral, ''affectional'', or spiritual, can suffer loss without injury to the whole.
{{right|Quoted in ''Sex and Education'', p. 172.}}}}

'''affectionate''' (a̤-fek′shọn-āt), ''a.'' [< ''affection'' + ''-ate''<sup>2</sup>; suggested by F. ''affectionné'', pp. of ''affectionner'': see ''affection'', ''v.''] '''1.''' Having great love or affection; warmly attached; fond; kind; loving: as, an ''affectionate'' brother.
{{smaller block|Her father appears to have been as bad a father as a very honest, ''affectionate'', and sweet-tempered man can well be.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Madame D’Arblay.}}}}
'''2†.''' Devoted in feeling; zealous.
{{smaller block|In their love of God, and desire to please him, men can never be too ''affectionate''.
{{right|''Bp. Sprat'', Sermons.}}}}
'''3.''' Characterized by or manifesting affection; possessing or indicating love; tender; warm-hearted: as, the ''affectionate'' care of a parent.
{{smaller block|He [Lord Russell] had sent to Kettlewell an ''affectionate'' message from the scaffold.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., xiv.}}
Victor Emmanuel was a man of strong family feeling and ''affectionate'' disposition.
{{right|''E. Dicey'', Victor Emmanuel, p. 152.}}}}
'''4†.''' Strongly disposed or inclined: with ''to''.
{{smaller block|''Affectionate'' to the war with France.
{{right|''Bacon'', Hist. of Hen. VII.}}}}
'''5†.''' Biased; partizan. = '''Syn.''' {{smaller|Warm-hearted, tender-hearted, attached, devoted.}}

'''affectionate†''' (a̤-fek′shọn-āt), ''v. t.'' or ''i.'' To affect; be affected, inclined, or disposed. {{smaller block|Be kindly ''affectionated'' one to another.
{{right|''Cambridge N. T.'', 1683 (Rom. xii. 10).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Give me but ten days respite, and I will reply,
Which or to whom myself ''affectionates.''</poem>
{{right|''Greene'', Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay.}}}}

'''affectionately''' (a̤-fek′shon-āt-li), ''adv.'' '''1.''' In an affectionate manner; with affection; fondly; tenderly; kindly.
{{smaller block|Being ''affectionately'' desirous of you. {{right|1 Thes. ii. 8.}}}}
'''2†.''' In a biased manner; in the manner of a partizan.
{{smaller block|He doth in that place ''affectionately'' and unjustly reprove both the Bishop of Rome and Alexandria.
{{right|''Abp. Whitgift'', Works, II. 185.}}}}

'''affectionateness''' (a̤-fek′shon-āt-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being affectionate; fondness; good will; affection.
{{smaller block|Dryden and Pope, however, kept their strength for satire and invective, and this style does not easily comport with hearty ''affectionateness.''
{{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXXXIX. 587.}}}}

'''affectioned''' (a̤-fek′shond), ''p. a.'' [< ''affection'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>. Cf. ''affectionate.''] '''1.''' Having a certain disposition of feeling; disposed. [Archaic.]
{{smaller block|Be kindly ''affectioned'' one to another. {{right|Rom. xii. 10.}}}}
{{smaller block|A man meanelie learned himselfe, but not meanely ''affectioned'' to set forward learning in others.
{{right|''Ascham'', The Scholemaster, p. 133.}}}}
'''2†.''' Affected; conceited.
{{smaller block|An ''affectioned'' ass, that cons state without book.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., ii. 3.}}}}

'''affectious†''' (a̤-fek′shus), ''a.'' [< ''affection'' + ''-ous.'' Cf. ''affectuous.''] Affectionate; cordial.
<poem>Therefore my deare, deare wife, and dearest sonnes,
Let me ingirt you with my last embrace:
And in your cheekes impresse a fare-well kisse,
Kisse of true kindness and ''affectious'' love.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tragedy of Nero'' (1607).}}}}

'''affective''' (ạ-fek′tiv), ''a.'' [< ML. ''affectivus'', < L. ''affectus'', pp. of ''afficere'', affect: see ''affect''<sup>2</sup>.] 1. Affecting or exciting emotion; suited to affect. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|A preacher more instructive than ''affective.''
{{right|''Bp. Burnet'', Own Times (1689), iv.}}}}

2. Pertaining to the affections; emotional.
{{smaller block|Without epilepsy she would have a condition of the ''affective'' power of the mind which is so deficient as to lessen responsibility. {{right|''Alien. and Neurol.'', VI. 375.}}}}

'''Affective quality.''' {{smaller|Same as ''affection'', 6.}}

'''affectively''' (ạ-fek′tiv-li), ''adv.'' In an affective manner; as regards the affections. [Rare.]

'''affector,''' ''n.'' See ''affecter.''

'''affectual†''' (ạ-fek′t̮ū-al), ''a.'' [< L. ''affectus'', mental disposition, desire (see ''affect''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.''), + ''-al.''] Pertaining to or consisting in disposition or desire; emotional; affectional; earnest.
{{smaller block|God hath beholden your ''affectuall'' devocyon fro heaven.
{{right|''Caxton'', Golden Legend, p. 389.}}}}
{{smaller block|Lust not only ''affectual'', but actual, is dispensed with.
{{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 205.}}}}

'''affectuous†''' (ạ-fek′t̮ū-us), ''a.'' [= F. ''affectueux'', < L. ''affectuosus'', < ''affectus'', affection, mood: see ''affect''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.''] Marked by passion or affection; earnest; affectionate; affecting: as, “made such ''affectuous'' labour,” ''Fabian'', vii.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
